The working girl, denied the privilege of
a normal, happy family life, can find in the
Rebecca Gratz Club a real home which is
something more than a mere boarding house
substitute for the parental roof. Attracted
by the title " Club" she comes to us with-
out a surrender of her independence, but
under the influence which permeates the
house she is gradually made a member of
the family group and learns the amenities
and responsibilities of such a position. Her
residence is not intended to be perma-
nent, but to last only while she makes the
illness or loss of relatives or economic stress.
The average number of girls living at the
Club is forty, but the turnover is fairly
rapid, and in the course of a few years
many hundreds of young lives are touched
